title: Tears are mercy
hook: the Prophet ﷺ wept at his son's death, and called tears a mercy (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, food for the bereaved, and the dinner made for Ja'far's family. Your line: feed the grieving. Did a plate leave your kitchen for someone else? Today, what to do when the grief comes out as tears. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

Even you, Messenger of Allah? That's the question, and it comes from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, one of the Prophet's companions. Anas ibn Malik was there and tells it, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had a baby son named Ibrahim, being nursed in the house of a blacksmith's family. Anas remembers the Prophet taking the boy, kissing him, holding him close. And then, some time later, they went in again, and Ibrahim was dying. The Prophet's eyes filled, and the tears ran. And his companion, watching, couldn't quite believe it. Even you?
screen: `EVEN YOU?` → `A BABY NAMED IBRAHIM.` → `THE PROPHET'S EYES FILLED.`

segments.voice: Some readers hear an old idea behind 'Abd al-Rahman's question: the strong one doesn't cry, and whoever is closest to God should be calm, composed, above all this. The Prophet's answer, in paraphrase, was simple: it is mercy. And then he wept more, and said, again in paraphrase: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord, and we are saddened by your parting, Ibrahim. Look at the shape of that sentence. Three parts. The eyes are allowed to cry. The heart is allowed to grieve. And the tongue is held: it says only what pleases God. That's the line the hadith draws. Not between crying and not crying. Between grief and protest. In another hadith in al-Bukhari, the Prophet's young grandchild is dying, and again his eyes overflow. Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah asks what this is. The answer, paraphrased: this is mercy that Allah has put in the hearts of His servants, and Allah is merciful to those of His servants who are merciful. So in that answer, tears aren't a weakness to be forgiven. They're the mercy itself, showing. And the line that is drawn? The same collection has the Prophet disowning, in paraphrase, those who slap their cheeks, tear their clothes and cry out with the wailing of the old days. Weeping, yes. Wailing that rages against what God has decreed, no. A heart that breaks, and a tongue that stays kind. That's the whole teaching, held in a father's tears.
screen: `EVEN YOU?` · `IT IS MERCY.` · `EYES WEEP, HEART GRIEVES, TONGUE IS KIND.` · `WEEPING, YES. WAILING, NO.`

segments.voice: The practice: let yourself cry, or at least let yourself be sad, if sadness is there. Sit, and breathe slowly. Is there a loss you've been holding tight, keeping composed about? A person, a place, a time of life. Let it come up, gently. If tears come, they come. If they don't, that's fine too. Just don't push it back down. Notice where it sits in your body. If you pray, you can hold the Prophet's words in mind: the eyes weep, the heart grieves, and the tongue says only what pleases the Lord. The bell holds the time.
Tears are mercy. The Prophet's answer when asked why he wept at his son's death: the tears are a mercy God places in the heart. Today's word.
Your line: tears are mercy. If you see someone cry today, don't hurry them to stop. Stay, and let it be mercy. Tomorrow, visiting graves. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims weep openly at deaths and funerals, citing the Prophet's tears at his son Ibrahim's death, while avoiding loud wailing, tearing clothes and words of protest against God's decree; his words about the eyes, the heart and the tongue are often recalled.

fork.setup: you're 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. the Prophet, whom you've seen stay calm through everything, is weeping over his dying son. what do you do?
options: tell everyone to leave the room.
fork.reveal: he asked, even you? and the Prophet answered: it is mercy, then said the eyes weep and the heart grieves.

original.note: Arabic: mercy, the word the Prophet gave for his tears.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Islam, a strong believer doesn't cry at a death.
what it means: the Prophet wept at his son's death and called the tears mercy; what's set aside is wailing and words of protest.
what a scholar hears: Anas's account of Ibrahim in al-Bukhari, the grandchild hadith with Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and the hadith on cheeks, clothes and the wailing of the old days.
